topic: Using concentrations of solutions in mol/dm 3 (chemistry only) (HT only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A bottle of sodium hydroxide solution is labelled 0.500 mol/dm³. What does this label tell you?
items.correct: Each 1 dm³ of the solution contains 0.500 mol of dissolved sodium hydroxide.
items.misconception: Each 1 dm³ of the solution contains 0.500 g of dissolved sodium hydroxide.
items.why: Both units end in '/dm³', which makes them look like alternative labels for one quantity, in the way that 'cm' and 'centimetres' are. Students also meet g/dm³ and mol/dm³ in the same lesson and copy the same number into both columns of a table. Moles and grams are different quantities, so the two concentrations are different numbers. The relative formula mass converts between them: concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × relative formula mass.
items.random_wrong: Each 1 cm³ of the solution contains 0.500 mol of sodium hydroxide.

items.q: A student measures out 25.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid solution. What volume, in dm³, must be used in a concentration calculation?
items.why: Students remember the factor 1000 but not its direction, and reason that a 'bigger' unit should give a bigger number. The same slip converts mol/dm³ to g/dm³ by multiplying by 1000 instead of by the relative formula mass. A decimetre cubed is larger than a cubic centimetre, so any volume contains fewer dm³ than cm³ and the number must get smaller. Divide by 1000 going from cm³ to dm³, and multiply by 1000 going the other way.

items.q: A sodium chloride solution has a concentration of 0.200 mol/dm³. What amount of sodium chloride, in mol, is present in 250 cm³ of this solution?
items.why: Volumes in the laboratory are always measured in cm³, so cm³ is the number the student has in front of them. The unit of concentration is written on the bottle rather than in the working, so its 'per dm³' part is easy to overlook. Read the unit of concentration first: mol/dm³ means moles in every 1 dm³, so the volume must be converted to dm³ by dividing by 1000 before it is used. An answer of 50 mol of solute in a quarter of a litre should also look impossible.

items.q: What mass of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in 500 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)
items.why: Volumes in the laboratory are always measured in cm³, so cm³ is the number the student has in front of them. The unit of concentration is written on the bottle rather than in the working, so its 'per dm³' part is easy to overlook. Read the unit of concentration first: mol/dm³ means moles in every 1 dm³, so the volume must be converted to dm³ by dividing by 1000 before it is used. An answer of 50 mol of solute in a quarter of a litre should also look impossible.

items.q: 4.9 g of sulfuric acid is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 500 cm³. What is the concentration of the solution, in mol/dm³? (Relative formula mass of H₂SO₄ = 98)
items.why: Both units end in '/dm³', which makes them look like alternative labels for one quantity, in the way that 'cm' and 'centimetres' are. Students also meet g/dm³ and mol/dm³ in the same lesson and copy the same number into both columns of a table. Moles and grams are different quantities, so the two concentrations are different numbers. The relative formula mass converts between them: concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × relative formula mass.

items.q: 5.85 g of sodium chloride is dissolved and made up to 250 cm³ of solution. The same mass is dissolved and made up to 1.00 dm³ of solution. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The 250 cm³ solution is the more concentrated, but both hold the same amount of solute.
items.misconception: The 1.00 dm³ solution is the more concentrated, because its volume of solution is larger.
items.why: 'More' is read as 'more concentrated'. Diagrams that show a large beaker of dark solution next to a small one reinforce the idea that size and strength go together. Concentration is a ratio, not a total. It compares the amount of solute with the volume of solution it is spread through, so a small flask can easily be more concentrated than a large one.
items.random_wrong: The two solutions have the same concentration, because the same mass of solute was used.

items.q: A sodium hydroxide solution has a concentration of 0.250 mol/dm³. What is its concentration in g/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)
items.why: Both units end in '/dm³', which makes them look like alternative labels for one quantity, in the way that 'cm' and 'centimetres' are. Students also meet g/dm³ and mol/dm³ in the same lesson and copy the same number into both columns of a table. Moles and grams are different quantities, so the two concentrations are different numbers. The relative formula mass converts between them: concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × relative formula mass.

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution, in mol/dm³?
items.why: Two volumes and one concentration are on the page, and the numbers are not labelled with the substance they belong to once they are copied into the working. The wrong pairing still gives a plausible-looking answer. Label every value with its substance before calculating. The first step uses the concentration and the volume of the same solution; the other volume is only used at the final step, for the solution whose concentration is unknown.

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 12.5 cm³ of sulfuric acid: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the sulfuric acid, in mol/dm³?
items.why: The shortcut works for every 1:1 example and is often half-remembered from a formula sheet. Because it removes the need to look at the equation, students stop reading the balancing numbers at all. The equality of concentration × volume only holds when the two solutes react in a 1:1 ratio. Always find the amount in moles of the known solution, then use the balancing numbers to get the amount of the other.

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What can be deduced about the two concentrations?
items.correct: The concentration of the acid is half the concentration of the alkali.
items.misconception: The acid and the alkali have the same concentration in mol/dm³.
items.why: Most worked examples in class use reactions in a 1:1 ratio, where equal volumes really do mean equal concentrations, and the balanced equation is never needed. The pattern is then generalised. Compare amounts in moles, not volumes. Work out the amount of the known solute, convert it using the mole ratio in the balanced equation, then divide by the volume of the other solution in dm³.
items.random_wrong: The concentration of the acid is twice that of the alkali.

items.q: A student pours 25.0 cm³ from a large bottle of potassium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.200 mol/dm³ into a conical flask. Which statement about the sample in the flask is correct?
items.correct: Its concentration is 0.200 mol/dm³ and it contains 0.00500 mol of solute.
items.misconception: Its concentration is less than 0.200 mol/dm³ because the sample is smaller.
items.why: Amount and concentration are again being merged. It is true that the sample contains less solute, and students transfer that reduction to the concentration as well. Concentration is a property of the solution itself, not of how much of it you take. Every portion of a well-mixed solution has the same amount of solute per dm³, however small the portion is.
items.random_wrong: Its concentration is 5.00 mol/dm³ because 0.200 × 25.0 cm³ works out at 5.00.

items.q: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 22.5 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution, in g/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)
items.why: Both units end in '/dm³', which makes them look like alternative labels for one quantity, in the way that 'cm' and 'centimetres' are. Students also meet g/dm³ and mol/dm³ in the same lesson and copy the same number into both columns of a table. Moles and grams are different quantities, so the two concentrations are different numbers. The relative formula mass converts between them: concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × relative formula mass.

items.q: 5.85 g of sodium chloride is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution. Water is then added to make 1.00 dm³ of solution. Has the amount of sodium chloride in the flask changed?
items.correct: No. There is still 0.100 mol of sodium chloride; only the concentration has changed, from 0.400 mol/dm³ to 0.100 mol/dm³.
items.misconception: Adding water to a solution reduces the amount of solute in it, because the solution becomes weaker.
items.why: Everyday language treats 'weaker' and 'less' as the same idea, and diluting a drink does make each mouthful contain less. The distinction between the total amount in the flask and the amount per dm³ is easily lost. No solute leaves the flask when water is added, so the amount in moles is unchanged. What changes is the volume of solution, and therefore the amount of solute per 1 dm³, which is the concentration.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A solution contains 0.0500 mol of sodium hydroxide (relative formula mass 40). What mass of sodium hydroxide is this?
items.correct: 2.00 g, because mass = amount × relative formula mass = 0.0500 × 40.
items.misconception: To get from moles to grams you divide the amount by the relative formula mass.
items.why: Students learn 'moles = mass ÷ Mr' first and then reuse the division when going the other way, instead of rearranging it. The very small answer this produces is rarely checked for sense. Moles and mass are linked by one relationship: mass = amount × relative formula mass, and amount = mass ÷ relative formula mass. Going from moles to grams multiplies, and the answer should be larger, not smaller.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two solutions are each made using 5.85 g of sodium chloride, one made up to 250 cm³ and the other to 1.00 dm³. Do they have the same concentration?
items.correct: No. Both contain 0.100 mol of sodium chloride, but the concentrations are 0.400 mol/dm³ and 0.100 mol/dm³, because the volumes of solution are different.
items.misconception: The concentration is decided by the mass of solute you weigh out, so the same mass always gives the same concentration.
items.why: Weighing out the solid is the step the student performs and remembers; making up to the mark feels like a procedural detail rather than part of the quantity being defined. Concentration in mol/dm³ depends on two things: the amount of solute, found from its mass and relative formula mass, and the volume of the solution it is dissolved in. Change either one and the concentration changes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: 4.00 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 500 cm³. Which volume is used to find the concentration in mol/dm³?
items.correct: The 500 cm³ of solution, that is 0.500 dm³, giving 0.100 ÷ 0.500 = 0.200 mol/dm³.
items.misconception: The volume in the calculation is the volume of water you added to dissolve the solid.
items.why: In practical work the water is what is poured in and noticed, and for dilute solutions the two volumes are nearly the same, so the distinction seems not to matter. Concentration in mol/dm³ is amount of solute per 1 dm³ of solution. The solution is made up to a marked volume in a volumetric flask, and it is that final volume of solution that is used.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many cm³ are there in 1 dm³?
items.misconception: There are 100 cm³ in 1 dm³, because there are 10 cm in a decimetre.
items.why: The conversion factor for lengths is applied once, or squared, instead of cubed. Students also recall '100' from the centi- prefix used for centimetres and metres. Cubing a length cubes the conversion factor: 1 dm³ = (10 cm)³ = 1000 cm³. It is worth checking against the familiar fact that 1 dm³ is 1 litre, which is 1000 cm³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the amount of solute in a given volume of solution found from the concentration in mol/dm³?
items.misconception: Because concentration is moles divided by volume, you divide the concentration by the volume to get the moles.
items.why: The division in the defining relationship is remembered, but the rearrangement is not carried out. Dividing by a volume smaller than 1 dm³ also makes the answer larger, which can look convincingly like 'more solute'. Rearranging concentration = amount ÷ volume gives amount = concentration × volume. Check the units: mol/dm³ multiplied by dm³ leaves mol, which is what is wanted.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, 0.00250 mol of sodium hydroxide reacts. What amount of sulfuric acid reacts?
items.correct: 0.00125 mol, because 2 mol of sodium hydroxide react with 1 mol of sulfuric acid, so the amount of acid is half the amount of alkali.
items.misconception: The 2 in front of NaOH means you multiply by 2 to get the amount of acid.
items.why: The balancing number is seen next to the substance being converted from, and multiplying feels like the natural use of it. Which way round the ratio goes is not checked against the equation. Read the ratio as a sentence: 1 mol of H₂SO₄ reacts with 2 mol of NaOH. So the amount of acid is the amount of alkali divided by 2, and the acid amount must come out smaller.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
